03 Core Curriculum

Microeconomics & Strategy

Lesson Lectures · learn

Finance valued the business. Microeconomics & strategy asks the prior question: how do people, firms, and prices actually behave when everyone is chasing their own self-interest at the same time? The answer turns out to be surprisingly orderly. Two engines run the whole show — incentives (what makes one person act) and games (what happens when your best move depends on someone else's). Master those two and you can read almost any market or competitive standoff. Tap the cards, diagrams, and quizzes as you go.

1 · The atom of economics: incentives

Economists don't assume people are greedy — they assume people respond to incentives: the rewards and punishments attached to each option. Change the incentive and you change the behavior, often overnight, even when speeches and laws failed. The cleanest illustration in the corpus is the British convict ships of 1787.

"Instead of paying captains for every prisoner who set sail for Australia, the government would only pay captains for prisoners who reached Australia alive. Overnight, the incentives of sea captains changed. The survival rate of prisoners reached 99%."

— Marginal Revolution University, "What are Incentives?" · in your corpus

Newspapers, clergy, and Parliament all demanded better treatment and got nowhere. One change to the payment rule fixed it. That is the economist's lens: don't ask people to be better — change what's rewarded.

No — and this is the subtle part. A benefit is anything you value (a hug, a view, a candy bar), and a cost is anything you give up, including the option you didn't pick. That forgone alternative is the opportunity cost — "what you give up to get something," as Nick Huntington-Klein puts it. Every real decision weighs benefits against costs including opportunity costs.

2 · Prices are messages: signals & the invisible hand

In a market nobody is in charge — yet skinny jeans get made and tablets reach the people who want them. The coordinator is price. A high price signals producers to make more and signals buyers to consume less; the two forces meet at a new equilibrium. CrashCourse names the mechanism:

"If people pay high prices for skinny jeans, that tells manufacturers, 'The company is very interested in skinny jeans, start making them.' If no one wants skinny jeans, manufacturers will start making something else instead."

— CrashCourse, "Markets, Efficiency, and Price Signals: Crash Course Economics #19" · in your corpus

Watch the loop in action. When demand for strawberries jumps, the price rises — and that single rising price does two jobs at once, pulling supply up and demand down until the gap (the excess demand) closes:

"This higher price first acts as a signal to communicate to producers that strawberries have gotten more expensive therefore this price acts as an incentive for producers to produce more strawberries."

— economiics, "Price Mechanism: Price as Signals & Incentives" · in your corpus

3 · The vocabulary — flip to learn

These are the exact terms you'll use to talk about markets and strategy. Tap a card to flip it.

4 · When your move depends on theirs: game theory

Markets coordinate strangers through price. But what about a handful of rivals watching each other — two airlines, two phone makers, two ice-cream carts? Now your best choice depends on their choice, and theirs on yours. That's game theory.

"Game theory is a mathematical theory that attempts to make sense of how it is that people interact in these strategic situations... the study of decision making under conditions of uncertainty over time."

— Big Think, "3 game theory tactics, explained" · in your corpus

The classic trap is the prisoner's dilemma: two players each do what's individually rational and both end up worse off. The corpus has a beautiful real case — the 1971 U.S. ban on TV cigarette ads. You'd expect a ban to hurt tobacco firms. It did the opposite.

The advertising game (two firms, A and B). Payoffs from 365 Financial Analyst's example: if neither advertises, each earns $50M. If both advertise, each earns only $40M (ads cancel out, but the spending is wasted). If just one advertises, it grabs share — $60M for the advertiser vs. $25M for the one who sat still.

Each firm reasons: "Whatever my rival does, I'm better off advertising" (60 > 50 if they don't; 40 > 25 if they do). So both advertise and both land at $40M — worse than the $50M they'd share if both stayed quiet. That stuck-but-worse outcome is the Nash equilibrium. The 1971 ban acted like a referee forcing the cooperative cell: ads off for everyone → profits rose.

"Both players are better off if they cooperate however they cannot be certain the other party will adhere so they opt for a solution that guarantees them the best possible outcome... companies will choose to advertise and that's precisely what happened in practice."

— 365 Financial Analyst, "Game theory lessons - Historical example: Tobacco companies" · in your corpus

5 · Why rivals huddle together: Nash equilibrium on the beach

Ever notice competing gas stations, coffee shops, and car dealers cluster on the same corner? Game theory explains it with the Hotelling beach model. Two ice-cream sellers on a mile-long beach should (for customers) sit at the quarter-marks. But each keeps inching toward the center to steal the other's customers — until both stand back-to-back in the middle. Neither can now improve by moving: that's a Nash equilibrium, even though customers at the ends now walk farther.

"You and your competitor's relative are in what game theorists call a position. Nash equilibrium is the point at which neither of you can improve the situation by changing the strategy from the original one."

— TED-Ed, "Why do competitors open their stores next to one another? - Jac de Haan" · in your corpus

6 · Two strategic mindsets: finite vs. infinite games

Zoom out from any single game and a deeper distinction appears. Simon Sinek splits all strategy into two types. A finite game has fixed rules, known players, and a winner — baseball. An infinite game has changing players and rules, and no finish line; the only goal is to keep playing. Business, he argues, is infinite — and firms that play it as if it were finite eventually burn out.

"The game of business is an infinite game... the number of companies that are playing finite they're playing to win they're playing to beat the quarter or the year and they're always frustrated by that company that has an amazing Vision a long-term Vision... over the long term that player will always win and the other player will run out of resources or the will."

— TED Archive, "What game theory teaches us about war | Simon Sinek" · in your corpus

The practical takeaway: know which game you're in before you pick a strategy. Optimizing for this quarter (finite) against a rival optimizing for the next decade (infinite) is how strong players get caught in a quagmire.

Strategy  =  (know the incentives)  ×  (read the other players)  ×  (know which game you're playing)

7 · The bias that wrecks good strategy: sunk cost

One human flaw quietly sabotages all of the above — the sunk cost fallacy: throwing good money (or time) after bad because of what you've already spent. Rationally, spent-and-unrecoverable resources should never enter a forward-looking decision. Big Think frames it through poker, then life:

"We'll often go to ourselves ah well I've gone this far I've put this much in I might as well see it through to the end but if you have very strong information that actually from this point onwards putting more money in the pot is a bad idea then you shouldn't."

— Big Think, "3 game theory tactics, explained" · in your corpus

Notice how Sections 1 and 7 connect: a sunk cost is the opposite of an opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is the future you forgo (always relevant); sunk cost is the past you can't recover (never relevant). Good strategists weigh the first and ignore the second.

8 · Check yourself

The British government couldn't reduce convict-ship deaths with laws or appeals. What finally worked?

Changing the incentive — pay on safe arrival, not departure — pushed the survival rate to 99% overnight. Change the reward, change the behavior.

Two firms both advertise and each ends up at $40M, when both staying quiet would have earned each $50M. What is this outcome called?

Each defects because advertising is individually best whatever the rival does — so both land in a stable but worse-for-everyone Nash equilibrium, the classic prisoner's dilemma.

You've read 100 pages of a book you're not enjoying. The "rational" reason to keep reading is…

The 100 pages are spent and unrecoverable — a sunk cost. A forward-looking decision ignores them and asks only: is the next page worth it?

⚠️ "The market will sort it out" — except when it won't

Price signals are powerful, but markets fail. CrashCourse is blunt: "most economists understand that markets are imperfect and that they often fail to meet society's needs." Price gouging, predatory pricing, pollution, and information gaps all distort the signal. Treat the invisible hand as a strong default, not a law of nature — sometimes a referee (regulation, or a ban like the 1971 ad rule) produces a better outcome than the unguided game.

🔎 One subtlety → your bridge to the next course

Everything here assumed players are rational and act on full information. Real humans cling to sunk costs, misread signals, and herd toward the center of the beach for reasons no spreadsheet predicts. That gap — between the rational agent of microeconomics and the messy, biased decider in the mirror — is exactly where behavioral economics and marketing pick up. Strategy tells you the optimal move; the next course asks why people so often don't make it.

🎯 Your move

Pick one rivalry you can observe this week — two coffee chains, two streaming services, two stores on the same block. Sketch the 2×2 payoff grid: what does each player gain if they cooperate vs. compete? Identify (1) the Nash equilibrium, (2) whether it's a prisoner's dilemma, and (3) whether the players are treating it as a finite or infinite game. You've just done a real competitive strategy analysis.

📚 From the Canon — Mankiw, Akerlof, Alchian-Demsetz & Jensen-Meckling on the economics of self-interest

This lesson taught incentives, price signals, and games assuming players are rational and see the same things. Four canon texts attack that last assumption. Mankiw sets the baseline — the real cost of any choice is the next-best option forgone. Akerlof shows what happens when buyers can't see quality. Alchian-Demsetz and Jensen-Meckling show what happens when you delegate work to someone whose interests aren't yours. Together they explain the warranties, audits, boards, and stock options that quietly run the business world.

Notice the through-line. Section 7 taught that a sunk cost is the past you can't recover; Mankiw's complement is opportunity cost — the future you forgo, which is always the real price of a choice. And the prisoner's dilemma from Section 4 has a quieter cousin: when one side simply knows more, the trade can fail before any game is played.

"Since the buyers can't tell the difference between a lemon and a plum, they won't be willing to pay more than what an average quality car is worth. But seeing that the buyers are only willing to pay for average quality, sellers of the highest quality cars — the plums — will exit the market."

— Marginal Revolution University, "Asymmetric Information and Used Cars" · in your corpus

The model predicts doom; reality routes around it. That escape hatch is Akerlof's three remedies made flesh — and it's why brands, warranties, and reviews exist at all:

"Some 40 million used cars are sold every year — more than three times the number of new cars… it means that over time the market has developed solutions… inspections, CARFAX reports, and certified pre-owned programs that offer buyers guarantees of quality."

— Marginal Revolution University, "Asymmetric Information and Used Cars" · in your corpus

Now flip from buyers-and-sellers to bosses-and-workers. The same hidden information becomes the principal–agent problem — and the punchline is that the damage isn't just a rip-off, it's the deal that never happens:

"The mechanic certainly knows more about car repair than you do… the bigger problem is that the potential for ripoff means that a transaction may be less likely to occur in the first place."

— Marginal Revolution University, "What Is the Principal-Agent Problem?" · in your corpus

Jensen-Meckling's warning is that the standard cure can manufacture the disease — option-heavy pay can create the risk-taking shareholders fear (think Enron, Madoff). Alchian-Demsetz add that the role is never fixed: a confusing org chart is usually a botched answer to "who can we measure, and how do we reward them?" Whenever you design comp, a board seat, or a vendor contract, you're answering that question whether you mean to or not.

Deeper sourcing — real quotes, counter-cases, and the corpus pushback — lives in the canon cluster notes: Akerlof on lemons, Alchian & Demsetz on the firm, Jensen & Meckling on agency theory, and Mankiw's principles.

Adrian: Hi, I'm Adrian Hill. Jacob: And I'm Jacob Clifford, and this is a crash course in economics. We are going to talk about a lot of things during the day. Everyone who wants a job has a job and production is in line with the ideal shared goals of society. But the reality regarding this was much less ideal for consumers in these companies. It turns out that people place greater importance on smartphones and good coffee than on tractors.

And so countries like China and Cuba moved away from broad central planning. Jacob: The problem with central planning is that it is inefficient. When economists talk about efficiency, they're talking about several types of efficiency that are different from the efficiency you might be familiar with. The first is production efficiency: the idea that products are produced at the minimum possible cost. This means that there is no waste of resources and raw materials and workers and machines are used to their maximum potential. Central planners, in general, are not so focused on price. But in the free market, private business owners have an incentive not to waste because they want to maximize profits.

In the words of Milton Friedman; "No one spends someone else's money as carefully as they spend their own." The second type of efficiency is called allocative efficiency, which means that the things we produce are the things that consumers really want. In other words, our limited resources are allocated to things we value. Let 's say a company only produces skinny jeans, then if it doesn't employ too many workers and if it doesn't end production with excess raw materials, then it produces at the lowest possible price which is what constitutes production efficiency. The problem is that it only makes skinny jeans.

Even if the company is efficient in production, it is probably inefficient in allocation. Consumers don't just want skinny jeans, some want bootcut jeans. Central planners will probably be less efficient at allocating because they have less information about what people want. Adrian: Consumer product manufacturers in the free market collect a lot of information about consumer preferences through tools like market research. But they can learn a lot about consumer desires by looking at prices. Economists call this price signaling. Let's go to the thought bubble. Okay, so if people pay high prices for skinny jeans, that tells manufacturers, "The company is very interested in skinny jeans, start making them." If no one wants skinny jeans, manufacturers will start making something else instead.

Here's another example: Tablets weren't really popular until Apple introduced the iPad. Then, boom! The market exploded. In fact, I know about 11% of you are watching this video on a tablet right now. Because I can see you. And I can't believe you're still wearing skinny jeans. When Google, Samsung, and Microsoft saw that Apple was selling millions of iPads for $500 and up, they had an incentive to enter the market. Price signals not only signal to manufacturers what to produce, they also help distribute tablets to people who value them. For example: If someone's grandmother doesn't really want a tablet and she was only willing to pay $20 for it, she won't get it.

Unless the grandchildren drag her into the 21st century by buying it for her for Christmas. Some economists love price signals so much that they argue with the tradition of gift-giving. This argument was popularized by economist Joel Waldfogel, who argued that gift-giving is inefficient. From a macroeconomic perspective, holiday shopping boosts consumer spending, GDP, and employment. But, if too many people buy products that the end consumer doesn't appreciate, then a lot of resources are wasted. Of course, this analysis does not take into account additional benefits of gift giving such as a symbol of love and appreciation between family and friends.

But the facts remain: the ideal gift in terms of effectiveness is cash. Money from the heart. Thank you, thought bubble. Theoretically, in a free market, producers cannot improve their situation without improving the situation of consumers. If a company produces too many units of a product or produces an unsolicited product, it will have to adapt quickly, or it will go bankrupt . Competition between businesses keeps prices and quality high. This is the invisible hand of our old friend Adam Smith. It 's important to take a step back here and point out that we are not saying that free markets are always good and that government intervention is always bad.

Most economists understand that markets are imperfect and that they often fail to meet society's needs. In these cases, economists encourage the government to create regulation or take direct control of markets to improve social welfare. In the United States, which is often mistakenly considered a free-market economy, it turns out that almost everything is regulated. For example, the FDA does not approve any wheat that contains nine milligrams or more of rodent excrement per kilogram. And the government directly controls the markets for national defense and public education. The field of public economics notices these things.

Now, I love rodent droppings and public education like the girl next door, but let's get back to markets and the role of prices in determining how we use our limited resources. So price signals help us use our resources efficiently, but that doesn't mean everyone agrees that it's always right or fair. Take the price gouging. Price gouging occurs when sellers raise prices for necessities such as food, water, or fuel. While there is something like an emergency. Some argue that this method exploits consumers and is an example of the cruelty of the markets. In the United States, anti-price gouging laws exist in 34 states.

But many economists say these laws encourage inefficiency and actually make the problem worse. They argue that letting prices rise during a crisis encourages others, outside the disaster area, to come in and sell essential goods. If there is no way to raise prices, then there is less incentive to bring those goods in. What’s more, high prices for things like batteries, sleeping bags, and generators mean that people who don’t really need them won’t buy them, making them more available to people who do. It’s not always government laws that limit price gouging. It may be the desire to make a profit that keeps prices low.

It’s clear that businesses can make a lot of money in the short term from price gouging, but what happens in the long term? Consumers will remember how they were treated. That’s part of the reason why some businesses like Walmart have an emergency operations center and a forecaster they employ to predict weather trends. It helps them hold Products like water and batteries in stock when they are needed. Not only is this profitable, it is also good for public relations. In fact, in some cases, such as Hurricane Katrina in 2005, private businesses responded faster than government agencies. Another example of how a pricing system is perceived as unfair is charging prices below cost.

This is called predatory pricing. It is the idea that a business can drive competitors out of business by charging low prices even at the cost of short-term losses . Competitors who cannot afford to keep prices that low will have to go out of business, giving those who remain market share and the ability to raise prices. Let's talk about Walmart again. Walmart has been sued dozens of times for predatory pricing. Their size allows them to pressure distributors and sell products at very low prices. Although many consumers like these low prices, it is bad for competitors. Especially for small, privately owned stores, which are sometimes forced out of business.

But is this predatory pricing? In the United States, The courts said no. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) website claims, "Although the FTC has examined the predatory pricing claims in depth, the courts, including the Supreme Court, have not accepted these claims." So predatory pricing lawsuits are common, but they rarely succeed in the U.S. In Germany, Walmart faced similar allegations in 2000 and was ordered to raise some of its prices. The company ended up leaving Germany in 2006. Predatory pricing is tricky and dangerous. When businesses are able to outbid their competitors by selling products at a loss, they will eventually have to raise prices above market prices to recoup those losses.

In the short term, consumers will have to pay more. But eventually, other businesses will see the high prices and enter the market. The end result is that there is no certainty that predatory pricing is profitable in the long run. Jacob: There are plenty of examples of corporate greed, inequality, and environmental neglect that make people think that markets are evil. And they are. Thanks for watching! See you next week! [Ending music] Wait, but there are also examples of socially conscious companies. That make an effort to protect the environment and help with the causes of cultivation. Capitalism, with its emphasis on price rather than fairness, is often described as the opposite of altruism .

But the two can, and do, coexist. But here's the big deal: Capitalism, with its system of price signals, is simply crowdfunding. We collectively choose what we want and how we want it to be when we spend our money. After all, companies can't force you to buy their stuff; they have to earn your money. So if you want to see real change in the world, don't just complain about corporations being greedy; expect more from them. We also need to expect more from ourselves. If you don't agree with the way a chain treats its employees, then don't shop there. Even if it has the lowest prices and the most convenient shipping options.

Of course, some of our social preferences come from governments, but they also come from each of us and the decisions we make about what we do with our time, energy, and money. It's also important to remember that it's a privilege to be able to have these conversations.

Why do competitors open their stores next to one another? - Jac de Haan

Translator: Ittirit Tweepholcharoen Reviewer: Kelwalin Dhanasarnsombut Why a gas station? Although it's located next to other gas stations. Why did I drive for miles without finding a single coffee shop? And then I came across three coffee shops on the same street corner. Why are grocery stores, auto repair shops, and restaurants often located together? Instead of distributing them evenly throughout the community. While there are many factors to consider when making a decision, Where should we do business? The clustering of similar businesses can be easily explained by “Hotelling’s Model of Spatial Competition.” Imagine you sell ice cream on a beach.

The beach is a mile long, and you have no competition. Where will you park your stroller? In order to maximize sales, walking half a mile down the beach might be too far for some. Located at both ends of the beach. But at this point, you'll be able to sell the most products to customers. One day you arrive at the same beach. You'll also discover that your cousin, Teddy, has brought his ice cream cart with him. Actually, he sells the same kind of ice cream you're selling. You two agreed to divide the beach area equally. To ensure that customers don't have to walk too far. You parked your cart a quarter mile south of the center of the beach, right in the middle of your area.

Teddy, meanwhile, parked his stroller a quarter mile north of the center of the beach. In the center of Teddy's area. Under this agreement... Your customers in the south will also buy ice cream from you. Customers who live north of Teddy will buy from Teddy. The remaining 50 percent of customers are in the middle. They would then walk to the nearest wheelchair. No customer will have to walk more than a quarter mile. And both vendors would each sell half of their goods to customers on the beach. Game theorists see this as... The "Socially Optimal Solution" (S.O.S.) reduces the maximum number of steps a customer needs to take.

In order to get to the ice cream truck, but the next day, when you arrived at work... You find Teddy has parked his stroller right in the centerline of the beach. As for you, you return to your original location, 1/4 mile south of the centerline. And you only get 25 percent of your customers who are in your south. Teddy still gets all the customers to eat above him. But now you have to split the remaining 25 percent of customers between the two carts. Day 3 of the Ice Cream War. You arrived at the beach earlier than usual. Then, park the stroller in the middle of Teddy's area. The assumption is that you will sell to 75 percent of all customers below you.

Leave your relatives to sell ice cream to only the remaining 25 percent of customers on the north side of the beach. When Teddy arrived. He parked his cart to your south. That means he's taking all the customers from the south. And that leaves you with only a few customers from the north. To prevent him from gaining an advantage. So you moved your cart 10 steps south to get the customers back. But while you're on your lunch break... Teddy moved his car another 10 steps south, and once again... He's stolen customers from the south again, just like before. And all day today. You both took turns moving the car south.

You walked towards the group of customers who wanted to buy ice cream, until finally, you both stopped in the middle of the beach. Turning their backs to each other. Each person sells 50 percent of the ice cream to customers on the beach. At this point, you and your competitor's relative are in what game theorists call a position. Nash equilibrium is the point at which neither of you can improve the situation. By changing the strategy from the original one. Your original strategy Where you two are right on the line. 1/4 mile from the centerline of the beach. I ca n't stay long. Because it's not "Nash equilibrium," you both can still move the carts closer together.

In order to sell more ice cream. Now that you two are both in the middle of the beach. You cannot move the cart to the furthest customer. Without making things more difficult for existing customers, however, at this point you no longer have a “society-satisfying solution” because of the customers at both ends of the beach. They had to walk an unnecessarily long distance just to get some dessert. Let's think about fast food restaurants, clothing stores, and mobile phone shops in a shopping mall. Customers would find it more convenient if these stores were more spread out. But this makes businesses vulnerable to fierce competition.

In the real world. Customers come from more than one direction. And businesses can compete with each other using marketing strategies. By differentiating your products. And with price cutting. But the core of those strategies is... Businesses want their competitors to be as "close" as possible.

What are Incentives?
Marginal Revolution University · 2:03 · 86,384 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~285 words

MRUniversity.com Learn Economics, Understand Your World Economics Glossary What is Incentive? What is encouragement? Incentives are rewards and punishments that motivate behavior. Incentives are everywhere. To better understand this critical economic concept, let's turn to the example of the British government hiring sea captains in 1787 to send convicts to Australia . The conditions on these ships were terrible. On one trip, more than a third of the men died, and the rest arrived beaten, hungry, and sick. The people were dissatisfied. Newspapers called for better conditions. Religious leaders appealed to the captains' sense of humanity, and the British Parliament passed laws demanding better treatment of these prisoners .

Unfortunately, none of these attempts were successful. The death rate remained shockingly high. But at that time, there was an economist who proposed a new solution. Instead of paying captains for every prisoner who set sail for Australia, the government would only pay captains for prisoners who reached Australia alive . Overnight, the incentives of sea captains changed. The survival rate of prisoners reached 99%. As one observer put it, “ Economics has defeated feelings and kindness.” As you can see, incentives are a fundamental economic concept that helps us predict human behavior. But incentives are not the only fundamental concept.
